To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the duration of the visual response to a light flash in the cat is related to the total duration of the flash and is not related to the duration of the flash at the time the response begins.
the duration of the primary response to a light flash is a measure of the duration of the light flash and that the duration of a train of after-potentials is a measure of its intensity.

(i) the duration of a visual after-discharge is inversely related to its amplitude and (ii) a flash of light to one eye evokes from both eyes an after-discharge that is of longer duration than that elicited by a flash to the same eye.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural limitations of visual excitabililty.
the study of the visual system in the cat.
the neural basis of visual perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perception of light is related not to the primary potential, but rather to the whole complex, or to the “primary potential plus the after-discharges”.
the neural mechanisms of visual excitability are limited by the duration of after-discharges in the visual cortex.
the visual system is capable of responding to light in a complex and orderly manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perception of visual stimuli depends not only on the primary response but also on the after-activity in the visual cortex.
the visual system is limited in its excitability.

the neural excitability of the visual system is limited by the capacity of the visual cortex to sustain a prolonged train of after-discharge potentials, which in turn are limited in duration by the time course of the after-potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain’s response to light is not just a simple reflex, but rather a complex process that is affected by many different factors, including the duration, intensity, and timing of the light stimulus, as well as the individual’s previous experience and expectations.
there are neural limitations of visual excitibility and that the duration of visual after-discharges can last for up to 500 msec.
we can now use a non-invasive technique to study the neural basis of perception.
